analysis.one_liner: Requires police agencies to report misconduct allegations, settlements, and their costs to a public federal database.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 24 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federal law enforcement agencies, and state and local agencies that receive federal justice grants, to report data on allegations of police misconduct — including use-of-force complaints, racial profiling, wrongful death, and the dollar amounts of judgments and settlements. The Justice Department would publish all of it in a searchable public database and issue annual summaries, and a state or local government that failed to report could lose up to 10% of its Byrne justice grant money. A Government Accountability Office study would analyze which agencies cost taxpayers the most.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and communities would learn, in one public searchable database, how much money police misconduct costs and who pays it — including when settlements are covered by the federal Judgment Fund or local insurance rather than a department's own budget [S3]. People harmed by misconduct, civil-rights groups, and local officials deciding on police reform would all get better data to work from [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities harmed by police misconduct

how_it_helps.text: Creates the first comprehensive national record of what police misconduct costs, requiring every federal law enforcement agency to report allegations of misconduct and the amounts paid in judgments and settlements each year.

Uses the federal purse to reach local police: any state or local government receiving Byrne JAG grant funds must collect and report the same kind of data or lose up to 10% of that allocation, with forfeited funds shifted to governments that comply.

Publishes everything in a public, searchable Justice Department database within a year of passage, updated annually, and requires DOJ to verify state and local reports against court records and newspaper accounts.
Reveals who actually pays for misconduct — the Judgment Fund, a department budget, bonds, or liability insurance — so taxpayers can see when settlements are shifted off department budgets.
Directs the Government Accountability Office to study the data after two years, identify the agencies spending the most on judgments and settlements, and recommend how agencies can reduce misconduct.

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies bear the cost of collecting and reporting the data, and state and local governments risk losing up to 10% of their Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds if they do not comply [S3]. No federal spending beyond DOJ's cost of building and maintaining the database is required [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies, via reporting and grant risk

drawbacks.text: The database counts unproven allegations — including anonymous ones by 'a member of the community' — alongside judgments and settlements, which could overstate misconduct and raise fairness concerns for officers, though the bill bars publication of officers' personally identifiable information.
The 10% Byrne JAG funding penalty falls on state and local governments, not individual departments, so communities could lose public-safety grant money over their governments' paperwork failures.

Collection and reporting would impose real administrative costs on thousands of small local agencies, and the data covers only allegations and payouts, not outcomes of investigations — so the public would see a cost ledger without a full picture of how cases were resolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a transparency measure: it changes no police conduct rules and creates no new liability, it just makes misconduct allegations and their dollar costs visible in one public place, with a modest enforcement tool (a 10% grant reduction) attached. The main costs are administrative burdens on thousands of agencies and the fairness concern of publishing data that includes unproven allegations, though officer identities are shielded. The main beneficiaries are taxpayers and communities, who currently have no national picture of what misconduct settlements cost or who pays them. It is a low-cost, high-information bill whose main obstacle was not its design but that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress without ever getting a hearing or a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Beyer introduced the bill on March 2, 2021, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
Twenty-four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; none of the House's Republicans did.
On May 18, 2021 the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it remained without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the 117th Congress.
The bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without either chamber acting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off: no public database of misconduct allegations and settlement costs was ever created, and no reporting requirements or grant penalties took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies, shielded from public scrutiny

for.name: Rep. Donald Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and submitted it to the House.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: House Judiciary Committee (chair: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 2, 2021 and took no further action on the bill — no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress, so the House never considered it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, but all 24 of its cosponsors were House Democrats and none were Republicans, and it sat without action in a Judiciary Committee run by a Democratic chairman.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local police departments)
industries.note: The bill would require these agencies to collect and publish detailed data on misconduct allegations, personnel actions, and settlement costs, and would expose which departments cost taxpayers the most. Their interest in avoiding this transparency runs against the public's interest in seeing it.

State and local governments would face new record-keeping duties tied to Byrne JAG grant money, with up to a 10% funding cut for noncompliance. Communities could lose grant funds if their governments do not report, but the same governments gain access to a national evidence base for reform.

The bill would put officer-level allegation categories, personnel actions, and settlement sources into a national public record, making patterns of misconduct harder to keep out of view. It excludes officers' personally identifiable information from publication.
